query: For high-entropy alloys intended for demanding engineering applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs the retention or loss of toughness, and why? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, the predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloys, the retention of toughness is governed by the stability of ductile grain boundary complexions. Trace additions of interfacial segregants (e.g., 1 at.% Boron) promote the formation of thin, amorphous intergranular films that absorb deformation energy and blunt crack tips, thereby delaying crack initiation and propagation.
generation.material_initial_state: A typical equiatomic high-entropy alloy (for example, CoCrFeMnNi) produced via conventional processing, with standard grain boundary chemistry and morphology.
generation.intervention: Introduce 1 at.% Boron into the alloy via controlled alloying and homogenization heat treatment designed to drive Boron segregation to grain boundaries.
generation.conditions: Mechanical testing under controlled loading (e.g., slow strain-rate fracture toughness tests, Charpy impact tests) conducted at room temperature and at moderately elevated temperatures (up to ~600 °C), combined with microstructural characterization (TEM and atom probe tomography) of grain boundaries.
generation.structural_mediator: Stabilized, thin amorphous or complex intergranular films (grain boundary complexions) enriched in Boron that develop along the grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Boron segregation lowers grain boundary energy and promotes the formation of ductile intergranular films. These films act as barriers to crack nucleation and propagation by absorbing local deformation and blunting crack tips, thus retaining or enhancing the overall toughness of the material.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline alloy (without Boron), the Boron-doped alloy will exhibit significantly higher fracture toughness as evidenced by enhanced crack initiation resistance (e.g., higher KIC and Charpy impact energies) and increased fracture strain. TEM and atom probe studies should reveal thicker, more continuous and chemically enriched grain boundary complexions.
generation.baseline: The same high-entropy alloy produced without Boron addition, which under otherwise identical processing conditions exhibits less stable and thinner grain boundary complexions, leading to lower toughness.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold for high-entropy alloys with structures (e.g., FCC) and processing conditions amenable to complexion transitions, particularly when the alloy microstructure is controlled to have significant grain boundary density. It may not apply if the material is dominated by a coarse-grained or single-phase microstructure with low boundary area, or if secondary brittle phases form due to excessive dopant levels.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal segregation concentration and the precise nature (amorphous versus ordered) of the grain boundary complexions remain uncertain. Additionally, interactions with other alloying elements or impurities may modulate the effectiveness of Boron in stabilizing these complexions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy alloy specimens using identical processing: one set with 1 at.% Boron addition and one set without any Boron. Subject both sets to identical homogenization heat treatments and then perform fracture toughness tests (e.g., KIC measurements and Charpy impact tests) at room temperature and elevated temperatures. In parallel, characterize the grain boundaries via transmission electron microscopy and atom probe tomography to evaluate the presence, thickness, and continuity of the intergranular films.
measurements: Grain boundary complexion thickness and chemical enrichment via TEM/APT
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Boron-doped alloy does not exhibit statistically significant improvements in fracture toughness (e.g., higher KIC, greater impact energy, increased fracture strain) relative to the baseline, or if no thicker, chemically distinct grain boundary complexions are observed, the hypothesis is rejected.
